newsitem.title: Netherlands: KLM GIVES EVIDENCE ON RADIOACTIVE CARGO.
newsitem.headline: KLM GIVES EVIDENCE ON RADIOACTIVE CARGO.

text.p: Dutch airline KLM began giving evidence on Tuesday at a closed hearing into the exposure of passengers to radiation on a London-bound flight last month, the transport ministry said.
It said the hearing, starting at 1200 GMT and expected to last around two hours, would seek KLM's version of events.
But a ministry spokesman said it was not expected to lead to a government decision today on whether to suspend the airline's permit to transport hazardous materials.

"A decision on the conditional withdrawal of KLM's permit to transport hazardous materials will depend on the outcome of the ministry's inquiry," spokesman Henk Houtman said, adding the ministry expected to complete its probe in about two weeks.
The Dutch transport ministry said on Sunday it was considering putting KLM on probation after the airline allegedly flouted legal regulations on transporting radioactive materials.
Probation would mean the withdrawal of KLM's permit to carry hazardous materials if it committed a second violation during an as yet unspecified trial period, it said.
The case arises from a shipment of slightly radioactive medical equipment on KLM's KL129 passenger flight from Amsterdam to London on May 2.
Routine checks on arrival by British inspectors showed the shipment, sent by a Dutch firm of medical equipment suppliers, emitted higher levels of radiation than indicated in freight documents.

KLM, which allegedly failed to carry out the required checks when accepting the cargo, had also seemingly failed to report the incident to Dutch civil aviation authorities, the ministry said on Sunday.
However this was vigorously denied by KLM's head of cargo, Jacques Ancher, who stressed that the levels of radiation had at all times remained far below Dutch and European safety norms.
